rules.rule: Deliver high contrast by default for all text and interactive elements: at least 4.5:1 for regular text and 3:1 for large text, without waiting for a setting to request it.
Never convey a state or information by color alone: supplement with an outline, pattern, indicator, text, or haptic feedback.
Accompany icons with a text label, especially on navigation and calls to action.
Give each touch target an active area of at least 48 × 48 dp, even if the visual is smaller.
Keep the interface usable with zoom up to 200%: no truncated text, no overlapping.
Regularly test main user journeys with assistive technologies and system accessibility settings enabled, during development and not only at the end of the project.
Expose progress indicators and state changes to screen readers with alternative text that describes what is happening.
Display dates, times, addresses, and phone numbers in local format, with no truncation or overflow.
Do not assume a color has the same meaning everywhere (red does not signal alert in all cultures); rely on non-chromatic signals.
Design and test for modest devices: screen 480 × 800 px or under 4 inches, limited storage, slow processor, older OS; offer a lightweight package.
Reduce data consumption (video, heavy visuals, auto-refresh) and give the user visibility and control over data-hungry features.
Indicate with an icon accompanied by a label which content remains usable offline, including when the device is still connected.
When network is unavailable, display an explicit state (icon and short text) rather than a blank screen or generic error.
Indicate file size next to any download action, so the user can make an informed decision about their data plan.
During a download, show progress and remaining time, allow pause and cancellation, then confirm completion.
Queue requests made without network, execute them when connection returns, and notify the user with a brief message.
Save form input locally so a network outage never loses what was typed.
In dark theme, use very dark gray instead of pure black for surfaces.
Write text in light gray rather than pure white on dark background to reduce glare on small text.
Desaturate and recalibrate accent colors for dark background while preserving their identity.
Express elevation in dark theme with increasingly lighter surfaces rather than shadows.
When the screen displays user content (photos, articles), keep a neutral, low-contrast interface that neither modifies nor competes with the content.
Build the palette as a regular tonal scale and assign each role a complementary tone that ensures readability regardless of source color.
Let the user choose the theme source color (manual selection or extraction from their wallpaper) and propagate it to the entire interface.
Specify all dimensions in density-independent units (dp, pt, CSS px) and provide raster assets for each targeted density multiplier.
Use motion to guide: establish a focal point, move shared elements to their new location during a transition.
Respond instantly to user input, accelerate and decelerate smoothly, with no abrupt starts or stops.
For bulk changes (multiple deletions in a grid), prefer simple collective motion and fade-out over individual crossing paths.
Prefer a single variable font over multiple static files to cover weights and widths, reducing download size.
Keep optical sizing active so headings, body, and captions use the design suited to their size.
Avoid tight letter-spacing in reading text; wider spacing reduces visual clutter and faint letters.
Choose typefaces where i, l, j, and 1 are unambiguously distinct.
Let readers adjust font, size, and spacing: no single typographic setting works for everyone.
Add sound or vibration only if it conveys useful information to the user; silence is the default.
The more frequent an interaction, the more subtle its sound or haptic feedback should be.
Encode haptic information through rhythm, intensity, and texture, synchronized with sound and visuals to signal progress.
Ensure all sound-conveyed information remains available in silent and vibration modes.
Design notification sounds that are brief, crisp, and unobtrusive, and alarms with gradually increasing volume.
Before designing voice interaction, verify it's better suited than a simple touch gesture.
Accept many natural phrasings of the same intent (yes, okay, sure...) rather than fixed commands.
Limit any voice-read list to three items, then offer to hear more.
On a device with a screen, read the first items and display the full list on-screen.
Test speech recognition with speakers representing target accents and language varieties; users shouldn't need to change their speech to be understood.
Start with a real human need before choosing machine learning; if an expert can't do the task, neither can the model.
The newer or more dynamic the feature, the more the interface must rely on familiar, reliable patterns.
Prototype the experience with real user content rather than waiting for a production model or testing with dummy data.
Process locally when possible and never leave the device without user consent.
Explain from the start what the system does well and how to use it, rather than presenting it as magic.
Give the user final say and full manual control alongside automation, with fine-tuning available one level deeper.
Make every indicator reflect the system's actual state, never just the intent of the command sent.
Don't trigger an avalanche of simultaneous alerts or reuse the same signal for multiple senses; group, prioritize, give each signal one meaning.
Organize commands to mirror the structure of the controlled system, so users form an accurate mental model.
Make the primary action larger, more colorful, and closer to where it's used, rather than burying it among secondary commands.
Don't sacrifice established interaction patterns (structured lists, action labels) for visual effect: expressiveness never compensates for lack of clarity.
Calibrate expressiveness by domain and audience (calmer for banking) and start from critical user journeys before choosing effects.
Use shape, color, size, motion, and container to prioritize and group, to evoke emotion without falling into cold minimalism.
Derive all variants (theme, language, density, screen size, accessibility) from the same foundation of rules and tokens rather than designing each context in isolation.
Justify each displayed element with a function; remove what doesn't have one.
Indicate a clear primary direction from the entry screen rather than multiple competing calls to action.
Don't present usage metrics (screen time) as a reproach or prescriptively; contextualize them and let the user decide.
Build in good defaults (limited interruptions, quiet at night) rather than shifting effort to the user.
Adapt tone to stakes: sober and direct for serious alerts, encouraging for activity goals.
Top each chart with a sentence that gives its conclusion and possible action, rather than listing raw numbers.
Start each design review by agreeing on the problem to solve, then assess each detail against that problem.
Tailor questions to the stage: problem and user at the start, hierarchy, layout, and motion midway, polish, jank, copy, accessibility, and localization after implementation.
Conduct the final review on a real build, on target devices, in multiple screen sizes and orientations.
Before fieldwork, study accessibility guidelines and try assistive technologies yourself (screen reader, keyboard only).
Recruit diverse participants in age, abilities, technical comfort, country, and devices, and test both isolated functions and end-to-end journeys.
Engage affected communities, especially underrepresented ones, in ideation, research, design, testing, and communication.
